Not a lawfag, or yours, but here is my take:

I would definitely read it through and then talk with any other company hiring you.

Non-compete typically means you can't work in an area where trade secrets may be shared from one job to another.

If your area is a "trade", that is a lot different than in R&D or even coding, so the laws may be more flexible.

For example, being a machinist for a high tech manufacturer working on parts is different than designing said parts.

The machinist typically follows plans and details, so if another machine shop took you on, you would still not be "working" in the same field as the other company - unless it was as a machinist for a rival high tech plant in the same field.

As a designer of a high tech parts, say for aircraft, the designer should be able to work for another designer, but not for aircraft, etc. (could get dicey, but the idea holds).

The spirit of a non-compete is that any knowledge you have at one company could not be used to give an advantage to another company.

This is where the courts have said that any broad non-compete agreements that prevent someone from doing any work in their field are unenforceable. Nobody can make you not work.

TL,DR: If you design computers for HP, you can't design computers at Dell. If you build rocket parts for SpaceX, you should be able to build suspensions at Toyota.
